**Theorem 6.1.** If \(T \in B(X)\) is an AC(\(\sigma\)) operator, then \(T\) is an AC operator (in the sense of Berkson and Gillespie), and hence there exist commuting well-bounded operators \(A, B \in B(X)\) such that \(T = A + iB\).

**Proof.** Suppose that \(T\) is an AC(\(\sigma\)) operator with a functional calculus map \(\Psi : \mathrm{AC}(\sigma) \to B(X)\). Let \(J \times K\) be any rectangle containing \(\sigma\). Define

\[
\hat{\Psi} : \mathrm{AC}_{\mathrm{HK}}(J \times K) \to B(X)
\]

by \(\hat{\Psi}(f) = \Psi(f|_{\sigma})\). It follows from Theorem 4.2 and [3, Lemma 4.5] that this map is a well-defined algebra homomorphism with

\[
\|\hat{\Psi}(f)\| \le \|\Psi\|\,\|f|_{\sigma}\|_{\mathrm{BV}(\sigma)} \le \|\Psi\|\,\|f\|_{\mathrm{BV}(J \times K)} \le 8\|\Psi\|\,\|f\|_{\mathrm{BV}_{\mathrm{HK}}(J \times K)}.
\]

It follows that \(T\) has an \(\mathrm{AC}_{\mathrm{HK}}(J \times K)\) functional calculus. □

The splitting into real and imaginary parts is necessarily unique if \(X\) is reflexive [4]. There are, however, examples on non-reflexive spaces of AC operators with more than one splitting of this type (see [6, Example 3.1]). Each such splitting gives a different \(\mathrm{AC}_{\mathrm{HK}}(J \times K)\) functional calculus. The situation for AC(\(\sigma\)) operators is less clear, however. An AC(\(\sigma\)) operator may still have more than one representation in the form \(A+iB\), but not all such representations give rise to an AC(\(\sigma\)) functional calculus. In particular, no example is known of an operator with more than one AC(\(\sigma\)) functional calculus.

It is not difficult to see that the class of AC(\(\sigma\)) operators is in fact strictly smaller than the class of AC operators. Lemma 4.1 of [3] shows that if \(T \in B(X)\) is an AC(\(\sigma\)) operator, then, for all \(\alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{C}\), \(\alpha T + \beta I\) is an AC(\(\sigma \alpha + \beta\)) operator. It follows that the example from [6] of an AC operator \(T\) such that \((1+i)T\) is not an AC operator also gives an example of an AC operator that is not an AC(\(\sigma\)) operator (for any \(\sigma\)).

One of the most important subclasses of AC operators has been the family of trigonometrically well-bounded operators. The following is a consequence of Corollary 5.7 and the definition of being trigonometrically well bounded [5].

**Theorem 6.2.** An operator \(T \in B(X)\) is a trigonometrically well-bounded operator if and only if it admits a weakly compact AC(\(T\)) functional calculus. In particular, if \(X\) is reflexive, then \(T\) is a trigonometrically well-bounded operator if and only if it is an AC(\(T\)) operator.

Brenden Ashton and Ian Doust
Abstract
A major obstacle in extending the theory of well-bounded operators to
cover operators whose spectrum is not necessarily real has been the lack
of a suitable variation norm applicable to functions deﬁned on an arbitrary
nonempty compact subset σ of the plane. In this paper we deﬁne a new Ba-
nach algebra BV (σ) of functions of bounded variation on such a set and show
that the function theoretic properties of this algebra make it better suited to
applications in spectral theory than those used previously.
Key words and phrases. Functions of bounded variation, absolutely continuous
functions, functional calculus, well-bounded operators, AC-operators.

Introduction
The motivation for this work lies in the spectral theory of linear operators on Banach
spaces. It has long been known that the possession of a suitable functional calculus
for an operator T on a Banach space X is often enough to ensure that T has some
sort of integral or sum representation with respect to a family of projections on X.
In 1960, Smart [15] introduced the class of well-bounded operators in order to
give a representation theory for operators whose integral representations were of a
conditional, rather than unconditional, nature. A bounded operator was said to
be well-bounded if it possesses an AC([a, b]) functional calculus (where AC([a, b])
denotes the absolutely continuous functions on the compact interval [a, b]).
On
reﬂexive spaces, all well-bounded operators possess an integral representation with
respect to a family of projections known as a spectral family. An account of the
theory of well-bounded operators can be found in [10].
A serious restriction of this theory is that it only handles operators whose spec-
trum is a subset of the real line. Attempts to address this problem were made in
even the earliest papers on well-bounded operators (see [13]). Over the past 40 years
a number of authors have examined classes of operators which generalize the well-
bounded theory to operators with complex spectrum ([5], [7], [8], [17]). Although
these theories have proved rather important in applications (especially the theory
of trigonometrically well-bounded operators developed in [8]), each has contained

**Corollary 3.2.** *Suppose that \(1 < p < \infty\) and that \(T\) is an AC-operator on \(L^p\). Suppose also that for all polynomials in \(z\) and \(\bar z\) on \(J \times K \subset \mathbb{C}\), \(\|g(T,\bar T)\| \le \|g\|_{AC(J\times K)}\). Then there exists \(C \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\|g(T,\bar T)\| \le C \|g\|_{C(\sigma(T))}\) for all such \(g\).*

In Hilbert spaces we can show that these functional calculus conditions are equivalent.

**Theorem 3.3.** *Suppose that \(T\) is a bounded operator on a Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\). Then the following conditions are equivalent:*

(i) \(T\) is normal;  
(ii) \(T\) possesses an isometric \(C(\sigma(T))\) functional calculus;  
(iii) \(T\) possesses a contractive functional calculus for the bounded Borel measurable functions on \(\sigma(T)\);  
(iv) there exist compact intervals \(J, K \subset \mathbb{R}\) such that \(T\) has a contractive \(C(J \times K)\) functional calculus;  
(v) there exist compact intervals \(J, K \subset \mathbb{R}\) such that \(T\) has a contractive \(BV(J \times K)\) functional calculus;  
(vi) there exist compact intervals \(J, K \subset \mathbb{R}\) such that \(T\) has a contractive \(AC(J \times K)\) functional calculus.

*Proof.* The equivalence of the first four conditions is standard. To show that (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (v), it suffices to note that for \(f \in BV(J \times K)\),

\[
\|f(T)\| \le \|f\|_{\mathcal B(\sigma(T))} \le \|f\|_{\mathcal B(J\times K)} \le \|f\|_{BV(J\times K)}.
\]

That (v) \(\Rightarrow\) (vi) is trivial. To show that (iv) \(\Rightarrow\) (i), one can proceed as in Theorem 3.1. In this case the existence of a contractive \(AC(J)\) functional calculus for \(U\) implies that \(U\) is self-adjoint (see [5], [4]). It is easy to check that if \(U\) and \(V\) are commuting self-adjoint operators, then \(T = U + iV\) is normal.

It is interesting to note that in general, it is not known whether an AC-operator on a reflexive Banach space (or more generally, an operator on any Banach space which can be written as \(T = U + iV\) with \(U\) and \(V\) commuting well-bounded operators of type (B)), must have a \(BV(J \times K)\) functional calculus.

Higher education has also dropped the ball when it comes to the other half of Lewin’s equation: the person.

The fact is that even if we somehow managed to AI-proof every classroom tomorrow, that wouldn’t be enough. AI is evolving at an astronomical pace, and even if an AI-proof environment could be constructed, who knows how long we could maintain it? Besides, cheating is a hallowed academic tradition. It didn’t begin with AI, and it certainly won’t end with AI.

So while we absolutely must address academic environments that make cheating easy or desirable, we must also develop people capable of exercising good judgment in difficult situations, like the one brought about by the advent and wide accessibility of AI.

Now yes, research has identified numerous traits linked to responsible, ethical use of AI: humility, self-efficacy, self-control, and critical thinking, to name but a few. However, it’s absurdly naive to assume that college students naturally possess these characteristics at levels sufficient to ensure responsible AI use. Such characteristics must be intentionally cultivated and reinforced—and yet higher education seems unwilling to acknowledge this.

For instance, at far too many institutions, “ethical development” seems to boil down to vague appeals to an honor code, forcing students to read Aristotle, Kant, and Aquinas, and, at least at religious schools, some variation of reminding students that Jesus is watching.

Now, there’s nothing inherently wrong with any of that. However, knowing Aristotelian ethics doesn’t make you an ethical person, which means ethical development has to be about more than just exposing students to information as if ethical development were a mere box to check. If we want to develop people who can responsibly use AI regardless of whether or not we can keep up with its vast potential for either avoiding necessary work or outright cheating, we have to be intentional about it. 

The good news is that higher education has an extraordinary opportunity for this process. Universities are communities of learning. Students spend years learning, working, and living alongside one another and their faculty. That gives us an enormous opportunity to cultivate the characteristics, habits, and norms necessary for responsible, ethical behavior. However, taking advantage of that opportunity will require a lot more intentionality than higher education is currently demonstrating.

As a social scientist, I’m reluctant to offer sweeping policy prescriptions. Universities differ enormously, and what works at one institution, or even in one department, might not work in another. Nevertheless, I think there are some concrete changes that addressing this problem is going to require.

First, higher education must get serious about changing the environments in which students operate.

First, higher education must get serious about changing the environments in which students operate. That means establishing clear, meaningful institutional standards regarding acceptable and unacceptable AI use and then actually enforcing them. It also means redesigning educational assessments so that students must demonstrate mastery of the material, focusing less on information regurgitation and more on whether students can understand, apply, and critically evaluate what they’ve learned. And no, simply relying on AI detectors isn’t going to cut it, as these technologies remain unreliable, particularly when used to make high-stakes decisions about students. 

Second, we’re going to have to reconsider how we evaluate and support faculty.

This means that student evaluations will probably need to go, at least as a basis for high-stakes personnel decisions. That doesn’t mean abandoning our assessment of teaching effectiveness—quite the opposite. We need to go beyond asking students whether they enjoyed a class or thought they learned something and actually determine whether effective teaching and learning occurred. This might require more resources, but will also allow for more effective teaching, less easily gamed assignments, and better faculty development. 

Finally, we’re going to have to invest in the intentional development of faculty and students alike, both around and beyond AI. 

This needn’t (mustn’t) be merely a vague aspiration. We know such development is possible, and we know what it looks like. It involves having students work through realistic ethical dilemmas, consider competing perspectives, practice strategies for making difficult decisions, and receive feedback on their judgment. Critically, these experiences can be incorporated into coursework, meaning that ethical development needn’t be relegated to occasional workshops or seminars. And even more importantly, we must assess whether these experiences actually work by measuring changes in students’ ethical judgment, rather than simply asking whether they enjoyed the experience. 

AI isn’t going away, and neither is the temptation to cheat.

AI isn’t going away, and neither is the temptation to cheat. We can spend the next decade playing technological whack-a-mole with students, implementing ever more elaborate safeguards while students keep finding ways around them, or we can actually fulfill higher education’s mission of creating environments that intentionally develop people capable of exercising ethical judgment even when shortcuts are easily available. 

None of this excuses students who cheat. But universities must also take responsibility for the environments they create and the people they’re supposed to develop.

Lewin gave us the equation nearly a century ago. It’s about time higher education started paying attention to both sides of it.

The Keller inequality is the Lp version of the well-known Lord Rayleygh problem: "What shape of drum produces the lowest note?”, but this time, the drum is a potential with fixed Lp norm. In the usual Schrödinger case, was solved by Faber and Krahn around 1920, and turns out to be equivalent to the Gagliardo-Niremberg inequality. However, the usual techniques do not apply to the Dirac case. In this talk, I will provide a novel technique which allows to tackle the problem both for Schrödinger and Dirac operators, and which provides interesting numerical schemes for this optimization problem. I will mention several open problems related to the Dirac case.

### 2.3 Applying Martin's (1992) three-perspective approach to organizational learning culture

Building on Martin's (1992) three-perspective approach, we apply integration, differentiation, and fragmentation as complementary analytical lenses to the conceptualization and investigation of organizational learning culture. The three perspectives illuminate different patterns through which learning-related meanings may be shared across an organization, consolidated within subgroups, or remain ambiguous and situational. Applying them to OLC therefore concerns not only the substantive content of learning-related assumptions, values, and norms but also the level and pattern at which these meanings are shared.
